Rust control flow is expression-oriented: if, match, and blocks all produce values. This removes a whole category of ceremony.

Functions

Gotcha: a trailing semicolon turns the expression into a statement returning (). fn f() -> i32 { a + b; } fails with error[E0308]: mismatched types and a note "expected i32, found ()". This is the single most common beginner error in Rust.

Everything is an expression

All arms of an if-expression must have the same type:

Functions that never return

! coerces to any type, which is why panic!() works in a match arm that must produce i32.

if / else if / else

No parentheses around the condition, braces always required (even for one line).

Loops

for works on anything implementing IntoIterator. Prefer it over while with an index — it cannot go out of bounds and it is faster (no bounds checks).

Loop labels

Labels are 'name: before the loop, break 'name / continue 'name inside.

match

match is exhaustive: the compiler proves every case is handled. Forgetting a variant of an enum is a compile error, which means adding a variant to an enum shows you every place that needs updating. This is the single biggest maintainability win in the language.

Matching structs and tuples

@ bindings and ref

match on Option and Result

if let and let else

When you only care about one pattern:

Rule of thumb: use match when you handle two or more cases, if let for one case with a fall-through, and let else when the fall-through is an early return. let else is usually the cleanest for validation.

The ? operator

Propagates errors (or None) and is by far the most-used piece of control flow in real Rust.

Full treatment in Error handling.

Recursion and stack depth

Rust has no guaranteed tail-call optimisation. Deep recursion overflows the stack (default 8 MB main thread, 2 MB spawned threads). For deep structures, write an explicit loop with a Vec stack, or use the stacker crate.

A worked example: a tiny expression evaluator

Control flow, match, recursion and Result in 40 lines.

Two subtleties worth noting:

  • matches!(self.peek(), Some(Token::Star)) avoids borrowing problems that a match on self.peek() inside a &mut self method would create.
  • let n = *n; self.pos += 1; copies the number out before mutating self, because the borrow from peek() is still alive.

Style notes that matter in review

Clippy catches most of these. Run it (module 03.04).

Exercises

  1. Write fn classify(n: i32) -> &'static str returning "negative", "zero", "small", "large" using a match with guards and ranges.
  2. Rewrite the evaluator to support / with division-by-zero returning an error instead of panicking.
  3. Add unary minus so -3 + 4 evaluates to 1.
  4. Write a loop that reads lines from stdin until the user types quit, accumulating a running total. Use break with a value to return the total.
  5. Convert a match with Some(x) => Some(f(x)), None => None into .map(f). Then convert a chain of if let into ?.
